en: The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai explains the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers. Regarding the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers":
"Tathāgata" has already been explained above. "Supernatural" (*shen*) means the unfathomable; "power" (*li*) means efficacious function. It is unfathomable...

Thus, the essence of the natural state is profound, and the power of its transformative function is great; because this section entrusts the profound Dharma and manifests ten kinds of great powers, it is titled "The Chapter on Spiritual Powers."
From this chapter downward, there are eight chapters in total, which constitute the entrustment and the circulation [of the teaching].

This present chapter clarifies how the bodhisattvas receive their mandate to propagate the sutra; the following chapter concerns the Tathāgata’s touching of their heads as he entrusts them with the legacy.
The text consists of prose and verse.
The prose is divided into three parts:
first, the Bodhisattva’s acceptance of the command; second, the Buddha’s manifestation of supernatural power; and third, the summary of the essentials and exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
First, the narrator describes the gestures of reverence; second, he makes a vow to propagate the sutra.
The propagation of the sutra is threefold:
first, the time period, which refers to the era after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Second, the location, which refers to the various lands of the emanated bodies;

third, the vow, which is not merely to benefit others by following orders, but also to personally aspire to this truly pure Great Dharma so that both self and others may be equally benefited and perfected.
From "At that time" onwards is the second section, which manifests ten supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). This is divided into two parts:
first, the assembly addressed; second, the actual manifestation of the supernatural powers.
"Mañjuśrī and others" refers to the assembly manifested through his provisional traces.
"Those who have long resided here" refers to the assembly originally transformed by him from the lower direction.
"All" refers to those who have come from other directions as well as those who have come from the emanation-bodies of the Buddhas.
Question:
Why do we see only those from the lower direction making their vows, while we do not see Mañjuśrī and others making theirs? Answer:
The preceding passage stated, "In my land there are naturally bodhisattvas who can uphold this sutra," which refers to obtaining both [the power of the tongue and the power of the voice].

Regarding the ten powers: first, the mark of the protruding tongue. As expounded in the present sutra, the three are opened to reveal the one; internally secret while externally manifesting; and the near is set aside to reveal the far. This clarifies that the benefit of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is entirely truthful and not in vain. While the tongues of those with merit reach their noses, and those of Buddhas of the Tripitaka reach the hairline, the present [tongue] reaches the Brahma Heaven, transcending the realm of ordinary beings and sages, and extending to the summit of the Pure Heavens. Since this mark is extraordinary, its teaching is all the more credible.

Second, light radiates from every pore of his entire body, illuminating the ten directions so that there is nowhere it does not shine brightly; this signifies the exhaustion of the realm of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya*).

Previously, the brilliance emitted from the ūrṇā-kośa began in the eastern direction, signifying the initial perception of the single principle through the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). Now that the present "Root Chapter" has concluded, he emits all-encompassing light that illumines all lands, enabling those at the initial cause to reach the ultimate Buddha-wisdom at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayak-bodhi*); the same applies to the various Buddhas who manifest as emanations.
The three coughs are the manner of one about to speak; they are also signs of unobstructed flow.

For over forty years, I have kept the truth concealed, but now it has been fully extended and expressed without any lingering impediment. This is the great matter of my appearance in the world reaching full completion; therefore, I cough. Desiring to entrust this Dharma to the Bodhisattvas so that they may guide and benefit sentient beings in future generations, I cough to announce this matter.
Coughing (*kṣveḍita*) possesses two meanings:
first, to clear away what has been said; second, to entrust it to others.
Fourth, snapping the fingers signifies sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).

I rejoice that those who follow the seven stages of expedient means enter together into the perfect path; I rejoice that through the perfect path wisdom increases and birth is diminished; I rejoice that all bodhisattvas uphold the truly pure Great Dharma; and I rejoice that future generations shall obtain the unsurpassed treasure.
This single snap of the fingers penetrates vertically through the three periods of time and extends horizontally across the ten directions.

Fifth, regarding the sixfold movement of the earth: this symbolizes the six successive movements of ignorance from the initial mind to the final mind; now, it further signifies that all people's six sense organs are moved so as to attain purity.
Sixth, the "Universal Vision of the Great Assembly" symbolizes that the Way of all Buddhas is identical, and from this point forward it shall likewise be so.

Previously, five thousand [monks] rose and departed, and during the three transformations they were moved away; having lost their original resolve, they could not receive immediate benefit. It is appropriate, therefore, to manifest extinction where there is no extinction, so that by following the various Bodhisattvas who propagate the sutra and attain the Way, they may enter the Buddha-wisdom no differently than in this present assembly. This also symbolizes the unity of those with the karmic capacity in the future.
7. As for the voice crying out from the sky, it signifies that in the future there will be one who possesses the teachings.
8. As for the phrase "Namo, I take refuge and am a disciple of the Buddha," it signifies that in the future there will be one who possesses human form.
Ninth, the scattering of various objects from afar as they gather like clouds signifies that there is one practice for the future.
Tenth, the ten directions being universally identical to a single buddha-field signifies the oneness of principle.
Question:
How is it known that the ten characteristics express the present intention and also express the future intention? Answer:

The text states: "By means of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, even though I have entrusted this sutra [to you], I am still unable to exhaust [its meaning]"; this clearly expresses and conveys its significance.
From "At that time, the Buddha addressed Upāriṣṭa" onwards is the third section, the summary and entrustment.
This text consists of four parts;
the first is the praise and entrustment.
2. Summary and Entrustment;
3. Exhortation and Entrustment;
4. Explanation of the Entrustment.
The initial praise is as stated in the text.
The summary contains four essential points:
"All dharmas" means that all are the Buddha-dharma; this summarizes the point that all are wondrous.
"All powers" refers to penetrating without obstruction and possessing the eight masteries; this is the wondrous function of the seal.
"All secret treasuries" refers to the fact that all places are universally the true mark (dharmatā); this is the wondrous essence of the seal.
"All profound matters" refers to cause and effect as profound matters; this is the wondrous tenet of the seal.

The phrase "all are proclaimed and expounded within this sutra" summarizes that this single scripture consists of nothing more than these four [sections], grasping its essential pivot and transmitting it.
From "Therefore, you all... onwards, there are three sections; these constitute the exhortation and entrustment, as per the text.
From "Why is this so? onwards, there are four sections; these constitute the explanation of the entrustment.

The preceding passage states, "Wherever this scripture is located, a stūpa should be erected. The essential points explained within the scripture are fourfold: "the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) explains the aforementioned profound matter;

"attaining bodhi" explains the aforementioned secret treasury; "turning the wheel of the Dharma" explains all aforementioned dharmas; and "entering nirvāṇa" explains the aforementioned supernormal powers. These four essentials encompass the entirety of the scriptural text; therefore, a stūpa should be erected at each of them.

As for what is essential: attaining bodhi is the dharma-body; turning the wheel of the Dharma is prajñā; entering nirvāṇa is liberation. These three dharmas constitute the secret treasury; that the Buddha dwells within it is precisely the meaning of a stūpa.

The *Āgama* states: "When a Buddha appears in the world, stupas are erected at only four locations: the place of birth, the place where he attained the Way, the place where he turned the Wheel of Dharma, and the place where he entered *nirvāṇa*."
"Sitting at the site of enlightenment is the place where the Dharma-body is born; all else is as stated in the text.
The verse consists of sixteen lines: the first four lines praise the ten powers (*daśa-bala*);
the subsequent twelve lines praise the summary of the essential points."
In the two lines following "Entrustment" (parindanā), the phrase "the merit of such a person" provides a general verse on the four dharmas.
From "one who can uphold [this] has already seen me" onwards, the second section consists of eight and a half lines, which provide individual verses on the four dharmas.
The first one and a half verses praise all dharmas, stating that "to uphold the Dharma is to uphold the body of the Buddha," and so forth.
The two verses beginning with "May I and my emanations" praise his supernatural power; through this supernatural power, he exhorts the Buddha to rejoice.
The single verse, "The Buddhas sit at the site of enlightenment," praises the secret essentials and is easy to understand.
The four verses beginning with "Regarding the meaning of all dharmas" praise matters of profound depth.
To preach the Dharma, shatter the darkness, and enter the One Vehicle—this is the profound matter of the Buddha.
The subsequent one and a half verses constitute the summary and conclusion.

Regarding the "Entrusting" (Zhūlèi) Chapter: "Entrust" (zhǔ) refers to that which the Buddha has committed to others; "cumulative" (lèi) means to trouble you with the propagation [of this teaching]. This name is derived from the sacred intent, hence it is called "Entrusting."

"Entrustment" (*niyojana*) refers to receiving the entrustment with the highest reverence; "commitment" (*parindana*) refers to accepting it with joy rather than weariness. These names are derived from the Bodhisattva’s respectful compliance; therefore, they are called "entrustment and commitment."

"Entrustment" (zhù) refers to that which was entrusted by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata; "bequeathing" (lèi) refers to that which is borne upon the head with sincere heart by the Bodhisattvas. Since this is discussed in terms of both the transmission and the reception, it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment and Bequeathing."

Therefore, the Tathāgata rose from his seat in person, extended his hand to stroke their heads, and bestowed upon them the Dharma that is difficult to encounter. The great assembly bowed deeply with palms joined; as instructed by the World-Honored One, they reverently accepted and vowed to practice it fully. For this reason, it is titled the "Chapter on the Entrustment."
The text consists of two parts: first, the entrustment; second, the joy of the assembly.
The first part has three sections:
one, the Tathāgata’s entrustment; two, the Bodhisattvas’ acceptance; three, the conclusion and dispersal.
The first section also has three parts:
first, the formal entrustment; second, the explanation of the entrustment; third, the admonition regarding the entrustment.

As for the formal entrustment: with the skillful hand of his single expedient wisdom, the Buddha stroked the crowns of the heads of all the Bodhisattvas of true wisdom who fill the voids of three thousand three hundred nayutas of lands.
Because the Tathāgata bestows the Way to transform others, it is called the Hand of Expedient Wisdom;
because the Bodhisattva practices the Way for their own realization, it is called the Summit of Real Wisdom.
To extend the hand and touch the crown of the head is the entrustment of one’s very person.
When expedient wisdom confronts ultimate wisdom, it is the entrustment through the mind.
"And he spoke these words" refers to the entrustment through speech.

This passage contains the intent of the four *siddhāntas*: "I have cultivated this dharma difficult to obtain over immeasurable kalpas"—having received and studied it from previous Buddhas, I now entrust it to you, and you shall in turn transmit it to others; thus the succession continues through the three periods of time—this is the *loka-siddhānta*.
"Universal dissemination with a single mind" refers to the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for the benefit of individuals).
"Causing [it] to increase extensively" refers to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial counteraction).
"Benefiting" refers to the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of the ultimate truth).
The section beginning with "Why is this so? explains the entrustment.
"Possessing great compassion" refers to the Tathāgata’s chamber;
"being free from all stinginess and parsimony" refers to the Tathāgata’s robe.
"Furthermore, being without fear" refers to the seat of the Tathāgata.
"The wisdom of the Buddha" is the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā);
"the wisdom of the Tathāgata" is the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (mārgajñatā).
“Natural wisdom” refers to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Within the Tathāgata’s chamber, he is able to bestow these three kinds of wisdom upon sentient beings; it is likewise so within his seat. Because he is such a donor, he is free from stinginess and free from fear. You all should train yourselves in this Dharma of the Tathāgata; this is called explaining the Buddha’s intention and entrusting [the teaching] to you.

The section beginning with "In future ages" is the entrustment. If there are those with deep roots, sharp wisdom, and upright intellect, one should explain the Buddha’s wisdom directly; if there are those who are not yet capable, one should instruct, benefit, and gladden them by means of other profound teachings.

The Buddha’s wisdom is profound and nothing else; the six stages of expedient means are other than profound; the sequential teaching of the Separate Vehicle is both other and profound. If you can employ these "other" and "profound" elements to assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s wisdom, you will skillfully repay the Buddha’s kindness; this is called the admonition and entrustment.
From "At that time, the bodhisattvas... onwards is the second reception.
Receiving with a joyful mind is the mental reception; "bending the body and lowering the head" is the physical reception;
"simultaneously raising their voices and speaking" is the verbal reception, which also implies the mental reception.
"Acting according to the World-Honored One's instruction" refers to receiving the intention of the Tathāgata’s chamber, which is great generosity;
"I shall fully carry it out" refers to receiving the intention of the Tathāgata’s robe, which is freedom from stinginess;
"May you have no concern" refers to receiving the intention of the Tathāgata’s seat, which is fearlessness.
The Buddha has thus entrusted [the teaching] three times, and the Bodhisattvas have accepted it three times, all exactly as described in the text.
From the passage "At that time, Śākyamuni... onwards, this is the third proclamation for dispersing the assembly.
Because Many Treasures came to bear witness to the sutra, and the two gates of the Trace and the Origin have now been concluded, he must be respectfully dismissed as he was before.
The emanated bodies gathered for the purpose of opening the stūpa; once the task of opening the stūpa was completed, they were ordered to return to their original forms.
Since the stūpa could not be opened twice, the emanated bodies departed and vanished from sight; yet because the stūpa continued to listen to the Dharma, it remained closed and in its place.
Question:
If one listens to the Dharma at a stūpa, it too should not be closed. Answer:
Because they have already realized the truth, [the Buddhas] have closed [their teaching]; because they wish for the Dharma to circulate, [the Bodhisattvas] remain, and so forth.
From the passage "When these words were spoken" onwards, it describes the great assembly’s joy.
The Buddhas rejoice because their work of transforming others has been accomplished; the Bodhisattvas rejoice because they have attained the Dharma for their own practice.
Furthermore, it is said that one rejoices because of the purity of persons; this refers to the Buddhas.
One rejoices because of hearing the pure Dharma; this refers to the sublime sutras.
One rejoices because of attaining realization through hearing the Dharma; this refers to those who obtain benefit in the present and the future.
Because these three matters were fulfilled, he was greatly rejoiced, and so forth.

[Commentary on] the "Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "Formerly named Jyotīrasa, he heard the exposition of the Buddha’s wisdom from the Venerable Sūryagarbha. He offered medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing: 'In the future, may I be able to cure the two illnesses—of body and mind—of all sentient beings. The entire world rejoiced and called him Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King)."

This passage clarifies that the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana suddenly renounced his body and further burned both his arms; regarding life lightly and the Dharma as paramount, he perished in body while the Way remained. By citing this past event to illuminate the present, it is therefore called the "Chapter on Past Deeds" (Benshi-pin).

If one examines this meaning, Jyotiska (Starlight) should follow after Priyadarśana (Joyful Sight), for he is called Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King) from the moment he made his vow upon relinquishing his medicinal herbs, and so forth.

The following five chapters all concern the propagation [of the Dharma] for the sake of others; this present chapter clarifies the teacher who converts others. It is because he desires that the Great Dharma be widely proclaimed and that sentient beings obtain great benefit that he exhausts his supernatural powers and his very life, his earnest and devout resolve remaining undiminished. He hopes that his disciples will revere the Dharma as he does, such that "I transmit the light to you, and you in turn transmit the light"—this unceasing transmission of light is the teacher's intent. Thus, we know that this chapter exhorts the teacher who propagates the Dharma.

As explained in the two chapters "The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" and "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara," the great beings from other directions receive the mandate to propagate this sutra; they universally manifest forms in various colors and shapes without fixed standard. These cannot be viewed with the eyes of cattle or sheep, nor can they be fathomed by the consciousness of ordinary people. One must not give rise to thoughts of contempt regarding what is heard; if one gives rise to such contemptuous thoughts, the Dharma will not permeate the mind. Therefore, we know that these lower sections of the text exhort the disciples who receive the Dharma.
Some say that in the preceding chapters the Buddhas perform Buddha-works, while in this chapter the Bodhisattvas perform Buddha-works.
This is merely a general observation; for there are also Bodhisattvas in the superior chapters, and likewise Buddhas in these inferior chapters, and so forth.

Now, it has been clarified that the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means) has completed its exposition of the perfect cause by opening up the three vehicles to reveal the One; the *Anrakugyō* (Chapter on Peaceful Practices) has explained the Dharma of riding upon the vehicle; and the *Juryō* (Chapter on the Lifespan) has completed its exposition of the fruit of the vehicle. In this present chapter, the person who rides the vehicle is explained. Thus, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states: "The Mahāyāna is that which is ridden by great beings such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī. The *Bhaiṣajyarāja* (Chapter on Medicine King) rides the vehicle through ascetic practices; *Gandavyūha* (Chapter on Wonderful Sound) and *Avalokiteśvara* (Chapter on Avalokiteśvara) ride the vehicle through samādhis; the *Dhāraṇī* (Chapter on Dhāraṇī) rides the vehicle through total retention (*dhāraṇī*); the *Sudarśana* (Chapter on Wonderful Adornment) rides the vehicle through vows; and *Samantabhadra* (Chapter on Samantabhadra) rides the vehicle through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). To interpret it in this way is convenient for the purpose of benefiting others and ensuring the circulation [of the teaching].
The text consists of four parts:
first, the question; second, the answer; third, the benefit; and fourth, the praise of excellence by Prabhūtaratna.
The question consists of three sections:
I. General inquiry regarding wandering and teaching; II. Specific inquiry regarding ascetic practices; III. Request for an answer, as in the text.
II. The answer is divided into two parts:
first, answering only regarding ascetic practices—whereas "wandering and teaching" refers here to the samādhi of the physical body, or to the [next] two chapters below.

Second, the praise of the sūtra. In response to the section on ascetic practices, there are first the clarification of the "basis of events" (*vṛttaka*), followed by the clarification of the "original event" (*pūrvayoga*) and the "basis of events," making three parts. These refer to the time, the Buddha, the śrāvakas, the land, and so forth, all as they appear in the text.
The original event consists of three parts: first, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma; second, the practice of offerings; and third, the reconciliation [of the past with the present].
However, since the Buddha acts universally for all beings, why would he favor only Priyadarśana?
This was merely a response to the occasion, necessitating that the teaching be entrusted for circulation—just as Śāriputra here represents the whole by speaking of a single part.
Asceticism is also twofold:
first, the present; second, the future. The present is also twofold:
First, attaining the Dharma through practice; second, forming the thought of repaying kindness.
Repaying kindness further has two aspects:
first, the power of samādhi; second, the power of the primary physical body.
The power of the body is threefold:
first, the burning of the body; second, the Buddha’s praise; and third, the timing.

Regarding "true Dharma offering," this refers to internally employing the contemplation of wisdom to observe the causes and effects of afflictions, using the wisdom of emptiness to dissolve them all; therefore, it is called the true Dharma.
Furthermore, one contemplates that whether it be the body or the fire, both the offerer and the offering are the true mark (*dharmatā*). Who burns and what is burned?
Since neither the offerer nor the offering can be apprehended, they are called the "True Dharma."
"Regarding 'all sentient beings' below, future ascetic practices are further divided into five parts:

first, birth into a royal family; second, recounting past events (*pūrvayoga*); third, approaching the Buddha; fourth, the Tathāgata’s entrustment; and fifth, receiving the command to uphold [the Dharma]."
All is as stated in the text.
There are four ways of sustaining [the Dharma]:
first, erecting stupas; second, burning one's arm; third, benefiting others; and fourth, manifesting retribution in this life.
Everything is as stated in the text.
From the words "The Buddha told" onwards is the third section, which correlates the past with the present.
This is further divided into two parts:
First, the summary; second, the exhortation to practice.

Regarding the exhortation to practice: it is superior to burn a single finger than to sacrifice one's external body, for the external is light while the internal is heavy, and thus their merit and blessings differ.
The text states that "wife and children" refers to external persons,
while "kingdoms, cities," and so forth, refer to external wealth.
From the passage beginning with "If, moreover, there is someone who [offers] the seven treasures," the text proceeds to praise this sutra:
First, he praises those who can uphold [the Dharma]; next, he praises the Dharma that is upheld; finally, he clarifies the profundity of the merit of such upholding.

To offer the seven treasures to the Four Noble Ones is not as good as upholding a single verse. The Dharma is the Teacher of the Sages; in its ability to give birth, nourish, perfect, and bring glory, nothing surpasses the Dharma. Therefore, people should hold the Dharma in high esteem rather than treating it lightly.
Below "Abiding King" (*Śrīkṣetra*), the second section praises the Dharma that is upheld, which is further divided into two parts:
first, praising the essence of the Dharma; second, praising the function of the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase, "Among all waters—such as streams, rivers, and great rivers—the ocean is foremost," the *Anantamukha-sūtra* states: "The four waters are a metaphor for the teachings, and within the 'Parable of the Medicinal Herbs,' the single cloud raining down is a metaphor for the preaching. Now, while all waters collectively represent the entirety of the teachings, the specific mention of these four types of water serves as a metaphor for the four flavors of the teachings: milk, curd, raw [milk], and cooked [milk].

This Dharma Flower teaching is like an ocean of *amṛta* (clarified butter). Its exposition of the ultimate fundamental ground is "profound," its pervasiveness throughout all places is "vast," and its exclusive elucidation of the Buddha-dharma without mentioning other teachings is "salty. Thus is the meaning of "most profound and vast."
The names of the ten jewel mountains appear in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and various other scriptures, and so forth.
Because the [inner] earth, the black [mountains], and the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) are not made of jewels;
although the ten mountains are indeed jewels, they are inhabited by either one or two types of *nāga* deities interspersed among them.

Mount Sumeru is composed of the four precious substances and is inhabited solely by devas; it serves as a metaphor for what is taught in other doctrines—the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and forty mental states (*citta*)—whether described as ordinary beings, sages, or saints, and whether their basis is said to be conventional, ultimate, or intermediate. These are considered inferior.

The truth of permanence, bliss, self, and purity taught in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is like that which is composed of the four precious substances; it is the basis for those who open, show, awaken to, and enter [the Dharma]. Therefore, this meaning is the most supreme.

The stars and the moon are both of the nature of yin and both appear at night; yet the stars do not undergo waning or waxing, and thus cannot equal the moon. While various sutras state that expedient wisdom lacks autonomy, this sutra clarifies that the expedient is itself the real and the real is itself the expedient. Their fullness and deficiency refer to one another, being two yet non-dual. To speak of expedient wisdom in this manner is superior to other teachings.

The sun is the essence of yang and alone can dispel darkness; likewise, while the various sutras clarify true wisdom to destroy delusions, they still do not equal that which is immediate in its reality yet provisional; how, then, could they be equal to that which is immediate in both its provisionality and its reality?
Therefore, one should know that this sutra clarifies that true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is the most supreme.

The commands of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) extend only to the four continents; those of Śakra reach only as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three; and the commands of Brahmā encompass both the realms above and below. This is analogous to what other sutras state: that the three truths and the three samādhis each do not subsume one another and cannot attain sovereignty.
What is taught in this sutra enters into the truth by means of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), definitively resolving the teachings for śrāvakas; it is the king of all sutras.
Entering into the conventional by means of the true mark, it does not conflict with any livelihood or worldly occupation.
Entering into the middle way by means of the true mark, there is no dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma.
The text says, "The father of all those in training and those beyond training, as well as those who have resolved their minds on Bodhisattvahood"; its meaning is thus.
Regarding the phrase, "The foremost among all ordinary beings, the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], and the pratyekabuddhas," this clarifies that he acts spontaneously and without effort.

In other sutras, one must rely on deliberate effort to enter the stream; for example, those who have attained the four fruits of the path only achieve awakening through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

This sutra, however, elucidates the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), which are not mixed with expedient means, such that one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience), as described in the passage beginning: "Like a great white ox, fat, strong, and powerful, its speed is like the wind," and so forth.
That śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are "foremost" clarifies that their cause is foremost.
Other sutras clarify that this cause consists of the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*);
however, the present sutra clarifies that the cause lies outside these expedient means, and is therefore foremost.
That "the Tathāgata is the foremost" clarifies the fruit.

While other sutras clarify the fruit as being proximate to the site of enlightenment (Śīla-maṇḍala), this sutra clarifies the fruit by pointing distantly to the original ground; therefore, it is the most supreme.

The section beginning with "This sutra can save" praises the function of the Dharma. First, it praises its function of uprooting suffering; next, it praises its function of bestowing happiness through twelve matters; and finally, it provides a conclusion.
All is as stated in the text.
From the passage beginning with "If a person should hear" onwards, the profound merit of upholding the sutra is clarified.
First, the merit of hearing the entire sutra is presented; second, the merit of hearing this specific chapter is presented.
There is a formal evaluation and a formal entrustment, as per the text.
That fragrant breath issues from the mouth is a reward in the present life; the rest are rewards in future lives.

Regarding the statement that one who hears this sutra will neither age nor die, this must be understood through contemplative insight: "not aging" refers to bliss (*sukha*), and "not dying" refers to permanence (*nitya*). By hearing this sutra, one attains the realization of permanence and bliss, remaining composed within and free from all fear or dread.
The section beginning with "He said this" is the third, concerning the benefits gained by those who hear the teaching, as explained in the text.
The fourth is the praise of "Much Treasure," also as in the text.

The *Pumen Pusa Pin* (Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara) is self-explanatory within its own text: in the past, he offered one hundred thousand kinds of music to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja; now, as he travels to transform other lands, musical instruments follow him of their own accord.
In the past, you offered eighty-four thousand precious bowls; now, you are surrounded by as many followers who serve as vessels for the Way.

In the past, you attained the *dhāraṇī* of the languages of all sentient beings; now, manifesting in forms according to the needs of beings, you roar with wondrous voices throughout the ten directions to widely proclaim this teaching. For these reasons, it is named the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound."

This chapter clarifies that by means of inconceivable power, the Bodhisattva interprets the scriptures in accordance with the various capacities of beings; those who perceive his traces cannot fathom his source. They merely savor his flavor without discriminating against its form; they should humble themselves at his station and allow their own currents to be dammed up. This is the second intention within the section on transforming others.

The text consists of six sections: first, the emission of light to summon from the east; second, the arrival from the west in response to the command; third, the propagation of the sutra throughout the ten directions; fourth, the benefits received in both lands; fifth, the return to one's native country; and sixth, the advancement on the path upon hearing this chapter.
The "marks of a great man" (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) constitute an ocean of great marks.

The merit of the hairs on the entire body does not equal the merit of a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana); the merit of all the secondary marks does not equal the merit of a single primary mark; the successive superiority of these marks from the bottom upward does not equal the merit of the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa); and the merit of the white tuft of hair does not equal the merit of the cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa). Therefore, these are the marks of a great man.

This manifestation of activity arises from filial obedience toward one's teachers and elders; now, by emitting this light, he summons his original disciples to propagate the sutras of the Middle Way and benefit those of great capacity.
The white tuft of hair arises from a single path of purity; now, by emitting this light, it causes this Dharma to be propagated extensively.
Question:
Since each and every mark of the Buddha is the ocean of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), why is there a distinction between superior and inferior?
Answer: This should be stated as it is clarified in other sūtras.
Question:

The Buddha’s disciples with whom he has a karmic connection fill the ten directions; for what reason does he summon those from the east to speak of the west, rather than addressing all eight directions?

Answer: This has a symbolic significance. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "For what purpose do the sun and moon travel over Jambudvīpa? It is because they wish to use their radiance to dispel the manifold darkness."
"The East is the beginning of light and the West is its end; only the Sage possesses both beginning and end.

This means that for those who have not yet resolved their minds, he causes them to resolve their minds; for those who have not yet reached the ultimate goal, he causes them to reach the ultimate goal. As it is with one bodhisattva, so it is with all the assembly; as it is in one direction, so it is in all directions. The Sage does not trouble himself with elaborate phrasing, citing one case to encompass all others; therefore, he speaks only of the East and the West.
The introduction consists of two parts:
first, the causes for the introduction; second, the actual introduction.
The causes for the introduction are sixfold:
First, the sūtra-author describes his merit and wisdom; second, being illuminated; third, the departure; fourth, the admonition; fifth, receiving the command; sixth, manifesting the signs of arrival.
The account of the source of his merit is due to his having encountered many previous Buddhas.
"Profound wisdom" refers to the adornment of wisdom, while the sixteen samādhis refer to the adornment of merit.
The description of the light illuminating his body and his taking leave of the Buddha is entirely as written in the text.

As for the Buddha’s admonition: since he was a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body, he achieved perfection without the need for formal discipline; however, because those in his retinue had not yet attained such realization, he used that occasion to provide a model for them.
The Buddha’s body corresponds to the ultimate principle; one must not perceive it as lowly and thereby forget its majesty—this is the admonition regarding the Tathāgata’s seat.

Furthermore, both teacher and disciple are fully endowed with wisdom and the severance of afflictions; yet the teacher manifests skillful means while the disciple likewise conceals their true reality—this is the admonition regarding the Tathāgata’s robe.

Now, the land of dependent retribution is entirely induced by the primary retribution; as the Tathāgata presides over the great trichiliocosm with compassion, one should attend equally to both the high and the low. Do not behold only the land of dependent retribution and neglect the primary retribution—this is the admonition concerning the Tathāgata’s chamber.
This Buddha’s extensive preaching of the sutra is also enjoined by three meanings; that Honored One’s admonition is that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.

As for "receiving the mandate": "the power of the Tathāgata" is the power of the seat; "the power of supernormal faculties" is the power of the hall; "the power of adornment" is the power of the robe. These constitute the great purport of receiving the extensive preaching of the sutra and the essential core for benefiting sentient beings; therefore, one is able to remain unmoved within this assembly while traveling to transform and guide throughout the ten directions.
The text on the manifestation of signs consists of six parts:
first, the dispatching of the lotus; second, the inquiry; third, the response; fourth, the request; fifth, the attribution of merit; and sixth, the command to come—all as set forth in the text.
Question:
If Mañjuśrī’s rank were lower, it would not be appropriate to seek an audience with him; yet if his manifestation comes as one of high rank, why is he suddenly not recognized?
Answer:
Although they occupy the same rank, there are beginnings, middles, and ends; if one does not understand even this single matter, one would be disgracing their high position.
Furthermore, seeing an auspicious omen among the assembly, he did not comprehend it and sought to give rise to understanding, which is why he questioned the Buddha.
From "At that time" onwards is the section on the arrival, which consists of six parts:

first, the journey with the retinue; second, the description of ascending the platform; third, the inquiry after health and the transmission of the message; fourth, the request to see Prabhūtaratna; fifth, the World-Honored One’s mediation; and sixth, the praise within the stupa—all as set forth in the text.
Third, the propagation of the sutra is divided into two parts:
the question and the answer.
First, the question regarding what roots of goodness were planted; second, the question regarding the existence of such supernatural power.
The roots of goodness concern the question of the past, while the supernormal powers concern the question of the present.

The Buddha responds to both intentions; the offering of music and the presentation of vessels from the past are linked to the present, all as stated in the text. This answers the question regarding the planting of those roots of goodness.
From "Huade" (Flower Virtue) downward, he answers the question regarding his supernatural powers.
He displays thirty-four ordinary bodies and four noble saintly bodies, which together constitute the ten dharma realms and the six paths of existence.

The section beginning with "At that time, Flower-Virtue" (*Puṣpadatta*) and following constitutes the inquiry as to which meditative concentration he currently dwells in to be able to provide such autonomous benefit; the Buddha’s response is as stated in the text.
The section beginning with "When this chapter was spoken" and following constitutes the fourth [section], concerning the benefit of the two lands.
Samādhi and dhāraṇī are identical in essence but differ in function: the function of quiescence is samādhi, while the function of retention is called dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, the manifestation of the form-body is called samādhi, and the eloquent exposition through voice is called dhāraṇī.

The Upper Grade states: "First, one attains the Samādhi of All Form-Bodies and transforms the body; one attains the Dhāraṇī of All Languages. One should know that sound is still a dharma of form; therefore, it is said that while their essence is one, their functions differ.

Furthermore, the purification of the tongue faculty is called *dhāraṇī*, while the purification of the remaining faculties is called *samādhi*; these are all gateways to the Dharma of the purification of the six sense faculties.
From the passage beginning "At that time, Gadgadasvara... onwards is the fifth section: returning to his original land.

Regarding the phrase "the earth shakes and flowers rain down": if even the experiences of a bodhisattva can provide incidental benefit, how much more so when the Buddha emits light before him, which shines incidentally upon one hundred and eight million nayutas of lands in the eastern direction—this too is an incidental discussion of benefit.
Sixth, the "Chapter on Hearing and Progressing in the Path," as in the text.

Regarding the *Exegesis of the Universal Gate Chapter of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*: this chapter is a core scripture of the present age, and there have been many lecturers upon it. My current explanation differs from others; there is a separate work in two volumes titled *Private Notes*, from which I have here briefly excerpted [the essentials].
In explaining this title, there are both general and specific aspects. There are ten pairs in the general sense and five single items in the specific sense.
As for the ten pairs, they range from the first, person and dharma, to the tenth, wisdom and abandonment, and so forth.
"Avalokiteśvara" refers to the person; "Universal Gate" refers to the Dharma.
There are many kinds of persons, and so forth; there are many kinds of dharmas, and so forth.

The preceding dialogue discusses the person who is Avalokiteśvara, while the subsequent dialogue discusses the Dharma of the Universal Gate; because the person and the Dharma are combined in the title, it is called the "Universal Gate Chapter on Avalokiteśvara."
Second, "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the Great Compassion that uproots suffering; based on the preceding dialogue, all hundreds of thousands of afflictions are liberated.
"Universal Gate" refers to the Great Benevolence that bestows happiness; based on the subsequent dialogue, he preaches the Dharma according to how each should be delivered.
Third, "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the adornment of wisdom; wisdom can sever delusions just as there is no darkness when it is bright.
"Universal Gate" refers to the adornment of merit; merit can transform one's lifespan just as a jewel rains down treasures.
Regarding "Avalokiteśvara" (Contemplating the World's Sounds), it refers to contemplating the profound within the objective realm; this is the Dharmakāya.
Regarding "Universal Gate," it refers to manifesting according to what is appropriate for each being; this is the Nirmāṇakāya.
5. "Avalokiteśvara" is like the king of medicinal trees, whose entire body heals all illnesses;
"Universal Gate" is like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels, which grants whatever one desires.

Regarding "Avalokiteśvara" (Guānshìyīn): it refers to working for benefit in secret, where there is nothing seen or heard; yet one is freed from the three poisons and the seven calamities, and both of the two types of seeking and the two types of vows are fulfilled.

Regarding "Universal Gateway" (Pǔmén): it refers to manifesting benefit, wherein one beholds with the eyes the countenances of the thirty-three holy ones and hears with the ears the teachings of the nineteen honored ones.
7. "Contemplating Avalokiteśvara" refers to the wisdom that illuminates reality according to one's own mind;
"Universal Gateway" refers to the wisdom of skillful means that illuminates according to the minds of others.

8. "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the immovability of the fundamental limit; "Universal Gate" refers to the traces that adapt to all forms and dimensions. 9. "Avalokiteśvara" means that the fundamental nature is the seed of the *vidyā-hetu* (the cause of realization);
"Universal Gate" means that the fundamental nature is the seed of the *pratyaya-hetu* (the causal condition).
10. "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the ultimate virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), like the moonlight on the fourteenth night;
"Universal Gate" (*Samantamukha*) refers to the ultimate virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), like the moon on the twenty-ninth night when its waning light is nearly exhausted.

The two questions and answers within the sūtra text contain immeasurable meanings; briefly employing ten pairs of categories, beginning from persons and dharmas and ending with wisdom and abandonment, the general title of this chapter is explained, its meaning being thus.
Regarding the separate discussion of the five aspects, the first is "contemplation" (guan).
There are many types of contemplation, namely: analytical contemplation, essential contemplation, sequential contemplation, and perfect contemplation.
Analytical contemplation (*vibhāga-vipaśyanā*) is the extinction of form to enter emptiness;
essential contemplation (*tattva-vipaśyanā*) is that form itself is emptiness;
sequential contemplation (*anupūrva-vipaśyanā*) refers to the progression from analytical contemplation up to perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*).

"Complete contemplation" (yuánguān) means that analytical contemplation (*xièguān*) is itself the true reality (*shíxiàng*), and even sequential contemplation (*cìdìguān*) is likewise the true reality.

Here, we exclude the three types of contemplation to discuss only complete contemplation; this is the meaning of the text’s reference to the "Universal Gate" (*pǔmén*). If the contemplation were not complete, the gate would not be called "universal. This is precisely that point.

Regarding "the world" (*loka*): if one examines it in terms of the sequence of past and future existences within the process of conditioned activity, or if one examines it in terms of the sequence of prior and subsequent [moments] in verbal expression, we shall here discuss the world last for the sake of convenience in exposition.

The world is also of many kinds, namely: the conditioned world (*saṃskṛta-loka*), the unconditioned world (*asaṃskṛta-loka*), the world of the two extremes (*antadvaya-loka*), and the inconceivable world (*acintya-loka*).

The conditioned world refers to the worlds of the three realms; the unconditioned world refers to the two types of nirvāṇa; the world of the two extremes refers to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; and the inconceivable world refers to the realm of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
To simplify all worlds, one takes only the inconceivable world.

"Sound" refers to the capacity (or faculty); there are many kinds of capacities: the capacity of humans and devas, the capacity of the two vehicles, the capacity of bodhisattvas, and the capacity of Buddhas.
For those with the faculties of humans and devas, it is: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good.
For those with the faculties of the Two Vehicles, it is: "To loathe and fear birth and death, and to rejoice in and esteem the unconditioned.
For those with the faculties of Bodhisattvas, it is: "To put others before oneself, and to be compassionate, benevolent, and yielding."
The "Buddha-organ" (buddhi) refers to entering all dharmas by means of universal contemplation; it is the unimpeded person who transcends birth and death through the single path.

Setting aside the organs of all other sounds and responding only to the organ of the Buddha-sound, because of this causal condition of organ and response, he is named "Avalokiteśvara" (Contemplator of the Sounds of the World).

"Universal" (*pǔ*) means all-pervasive. All phenomena (*dharmas*) are immeasurable; if one does not attain the universal, it is a partial teaching, whereas if one attains the universal, it is a perfect teaching. Thus, the *Siyi jing* (Saṃghāṭa-sūtra) states: "All phenomena are deviant; all phenomena are correct. Briefly summarized through ten aspects, one clarifies this universality. Having grasped this intent, one understands that there are no phenomena that are not universal. These are: the universality of compassion, the universality of the great vows, the universality of practice, the universality of leaving delusion behind, the universality of entering the Dharma-gates, the universality of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), the universality of skillful means (*upāya*), the universality of preaching the Dharma, the universality of maturing sentient beings, and the universality of making offerings to all Buddhas. Beginning with humans and devas and ending with Bodhisattvas, all possess compassion; yet, some are universal while others are not.
Since the essence of compassion directed toward sentient beings and dharmas relies on dual conditions, its scope is partial; because its objects are not extensive, it cannot be called universal.
Compassion that is objectless (anālambana) shares the same essence as true reality (dharmatā); since its principle is perfect, there is nowhere it does not pervade.
Just as a magnet attracts iron through spontaneous correspondence, so too does this compassion universally permeate all things; thus it is called "universal compassion.

Regarding "universal great vow" (*mahāpraṇidhāna*): "great" (*mahā*) means vast, and "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) means to restrain; because one extensively restrains and governs the essential mind, it is called a "great vow."

The great vow arises in relation to the Four Noble Truths. If it were restricted to the four truths of conditioned arising, non-arising, and the immeasurable, it would not encompass all phenomena exhaustively and thus could not be called "universal.
However, if it is based on the unconditioned Four Noble Truths, it is termed the "universality of the great vow."

Regarding the universal nature of practice: for example, prior to encountering Dīpaṃkara Buddha, whatever the Buddha practiced was not in accord with ultimate principle. Once he received the prediction of his future enlightenment, however, every encounter with phenomena was immediately the principle itself. For one who practices by traversing all phenomena through the union of principle and wisdom, there is no practice that is not universal.

Regarding the universality of severing delusions: if one employs the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) or the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) to sever the four abodes of existence and the delusions as numerous as motes of dust, it is like pruning branches and twigs; this is not called the universality of severing delusions.

If, however, one employs the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) to sever ignorance (*avidyā*), such that all five abodes are exhausted as if the very root were removed, this is called the universality of severing delusions.
Regarding "entering the universal Dharma-gate": that which precedes the Path is called the cultivation of skillful means; that which is entered after the Path is called entering the Dharma-gate.

If those of the Two Vehicles enter a single samādhi with a single mind, they achieve only one thing with that single mind and cannot attain many; furthermore, because they are bound by their concentration, it is not called "universal.
If one passes through the various stages in their distinct order of shallow and deep gradations, this too is not called "universal."

If one enters the King Samādhi, all samādhis enter therein; without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation, one manifests all modes of dignified conduct. Therefore, it is called the Universal Dharma Gate.

Regarding "universal supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*): the *divyacakṣus* of a great arhat illuminates a trichiliocosm; that of a pratyekabuddha illuminates a hundred buddha-worlds; and that of a bodhisattva illuminates worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. In all these cases, because they take limited objects as their conditions, the manifestation of their powers is likewise partial.

If one cultivates them by taking the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the object, then with a single manifestation, everything is manifested. If even the semblance of such powers—as described above—is universal, how much more so the actual supernormal powers? How could they not be universal?

Skillful means (*upāya*) are universally pervasive in two ways. First, those prior to the Path are subsumed within the practice of the Path itself. Second, those subsequent to the Path are also twofold:
first, the essence of the Dharma, as explained in the "Entry into the Dharma Gate"; second, the transformative function, as explained here.

This involves responding to the capacities of beings and benefiting them by being perfectly and simultaneously adapted to their conditions and needs. Although there are various modes of activity, they do not diminish the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the Dharma-nature; this is called the universal pervasiveness of skillful means.

Regarding the universality of preaching the Dharma: one is able to use a single sublime voice to accord with the capacities of the ten dharma realms, enabling all beings according to their respective natures and types to attain liberation, just like the lute of the asuras; therefore, it is called the universality of preaching the Dharma.

Regarding the universality of maturing sentient beings: all activities, both mundane and supramundane, are performed by Bodhisattvas. Whether it be digging wells, constructing boats, Shen Nong tasting medicinal herbs, or providing the benefits of cloud-shade and sun-light, they bring benefit to sentient beings, even extending to benefiting all worthies and sages. By demonstrating, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them, they lead them into the three types of enlightenment; this is called the universality of maturing sentient beings.

Regarding "making offerings universally to all Buddhas": if one performs external offerings, by means of a single meal, a single flower, or a single incense offered at one time, one makes universal offerings to all Buddhas; there is no before or after, as they are offered equally at once. It is likewise with the emergence of various kinds of dust from within a single atom.

If one practices internal contemplation, perfect wisdom guides all practices; this perfect wisdom is called the Buddha. All practices sustain this perfect wisdom, which is itself the offering to the Buddha. If practices sustain other forms of knowledge, it is not called "universal offering. When all practices sustain perfect wisdom, this is called "universal offering."

Regarding the "gate": when one enters from the conventional into emptiness, emptiness is unobstructed while the conventional is obstructed; when one enters from emptiness into the conventional, the conventional is unobstructed while emptiness is obstructed. If one is unobstructed only in one direction, it is not universal; because it is obstructed, it is not a gate. The Middle Way is neither empty nor conventional;
because it correctly penetrates the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and simultaneously illuminates the two truths, it is called "universal. Because it is correctly penetrating, it is called a "gate."
The meaning of the universal gate of perfect penetration is immeasurable; however, by briefly citing ten categories, it may be understood.
This chapter further demonstrates the universal manifestation samādhi as a means of transforming others and ensuring the circulation of the teaching.
The text consists of three parts:
first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the benefit derived from hearing this chapter.
The question and answer comprise two sections.
The first section of questions is divided into two parts:

first, the narrator’s account of the time, which concludes with the description of the bodhisattvas of the east and begins the description of the bodhisattvas of the west; this is the first [subdivision].
First, the explanation of the arising of goodness in the East is concluded; next, the second [section], the explanation of the arising of goodness in the West, follows.
Second, the explanation of the severing of doubt in the East is concluded; next, the third [section], the explanation of the severing of doubt in the West, follows.
Having finished explaining the attainment of the Way in the eastern direction, the fourth section concerning the time of attaining the Way in the western direction is now explained.

Regarding the term "Akṣayamati" (Inexhaustible Intention): the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that emptiness is inexhaustible; the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* clarifies the eighty gates of the inexhaustible; and the *Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra* states, "That which is inexhaustible is neither exhausted nor non-exhausted, and is therefore called 'inexhaustible'."
Taken together, these three sutras employ the three contemplations and the three wisdoms to explain inexhaustibility.
"Intention" (*manas*) refers to wisdom, while "inexhaustibility" refers to the objective realm.

When wisdom accords with its object, if one considers only the object, it should be called "inexhaustible"; if one considers only the wisdom, it should be called "intention. Because the object and wisdom are spoken of in combination, it is termed "Inexhaustible Intention" (*Akṣayamati*).
First, furthermore, the mind is the foundation of both the mundane and the supramundane.
Second, furthermore, the mind is the Middle Way within the Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that being able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the supreme concentration.
Third, this explains the name by way of the three types of wisdom and the three contemplations.
Regarding the posing of the question, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One who possesses the two adornments is able to both ask questions and provide answers."
Akṣayamati previously questioned Avalokiteśvara regarding the adornment of wisdom; the Buddha now answers Avalokiteśvara regarding the adornment of wisdom.
The Buddha’s response consists of three parts:
first, a general response; second, a specific response; and third, a response that encourages the upholding of the name. The general response is further divided into four sections:
First, the number of people; second, the encounter with suffering; third, hearing the name and title; and fourth, attaining liberation.

Regarding the various forms of suffering themselves: there is one person experiencing much suffering, many people experiencing a single suffering, one person experiencing many sufferings, and one person experiencing little suffering.
The present text mentions "hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions of sentient beings," which indicates a great number;
they "undergo various sufferings and afflictions," which indicates a great amount of suffering.
By citing the many to illustrate the few, it shows that if [the Buddha] can save even those with so much suffering, how much more so those with little!
Encountering suffering is evil, while invoking the name is good; the union of good and evil constitutes the meaning of "the occasion" (*ki*).

That "one attains liberation" is the "response" (*ō*). This is named Avalokiteśvara due to the causal conditions of such an occasion and response; it is also named Avalokiteśvara due to the causal conditions of person and dharma, and even due to the causal conditions of wisdom and abandonment.
Subsequent examples are treated in this manner; their names are established here to avoid further elaboration in the text.
The specific responses are threefold:
first, response to vocal stimuli; second, response to mental stimuli; and third, response to physical stimuli.
The section on the mouth is further divided into two parts: first, an explanation of the seven calamities; second, the conclusion.
Within the calamity of fire, there are four sub-sections:
First, holding the name is good; second, encountering fire is evil; third, the response; fourth, the conclusion.
Within this single difficulty, there are three sections by analogy:
first, the fire of karmic retribution; from the hells upward to the First Dhyāna heaven downward, all are discussed in terms of the capacity for the response.

Second, the fire of evil karma: from the hells up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, all are discussed in terms of the responsive manifestation of the capacity [of sentient beings].

Third, the fire of afflictions: from the hells up to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), all are discussed in terms of the responsive manifestation of the capacity [of sentient beings].
The seven calamities, the three poisons, and the two pursuits are all to be understood by this same principle.
Since this meaning is extensive, it can be known through the mind but cannot be fully recorded in writing.
The bodily faculties constitute the two [aspects]:
First, the two requests; next, the conclusion.

Regarding the request for a son, there is the establishment of vows and the cultivation of meritorious deeds; regarding the request for a daughter, the text on the cultivation of practice is abbreviated. This is because the act of prostration is identical in both cases, and thus it is omitted;
however, because the vows and the specific activities differ, they are set forth separately.
The "conclusion" (kṣepa) is as in the text.
From the passage beginning with "Therefore, sentient beings" onwards, this is the exhortation to uphold the name, which is threefold:
the exhortation to uphold, the comparative evaluation, and the concluding praise.

The aforementioned names of victory and virtues do not distinguish between form and substance; if one wishes to take refuge and revere them, one should maintain their names, and for this reason, I exhort you to uphold them.

The *Mahāyānāvatāra-śāstra* states: "The Dharma-body is one, while its manifested forms are many. This accounts for the sixty-two billion manifestations, all of which are equal to the single Dharma-body.
The Wise One said:
"The person of perfect realization is one, while those of partial realization are many"; thus, sixty-two billion persons of partial realization are equal to a single person of perfect realization.
The second set of questions is threefold:
"How does one travel? asks of the body; "How does one speak? asks of the mouth; and "Skillful means" asks of the mind.
This is the sage’s strategy of non-deliberative secrecy, which adapts to circumstances as they arise.
The Buddha’s reply is likewise threefold:
first, a specific answer; second, a general answer; and third, an exhortation to make offerings.
"Should employ" answers the question regarding the power of skillful means;
"manifesting bodies" answers the question regarding his travels;
and "preaching the Dharma" answers the question regarding his speech.
There are, in total, thirty-three bodies and nineteen modes of preaching, and so forth.
From the section on "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) downward, the specific [explanations] conclude by subsuming the general.
While the specific texts are extensive in detail but narrow in scope, the general response is concise in text but vast in meaning, and so forth.
From the words "For this reason" (*tasmāt*) onwards, there is an exhortation to make offerings.
Herein, because one beholds the physical form and hears the Dharma, one is exhorted to make offerings.
First, the exhortation; second, the acceptance of the instruction.
The acceptance of the mandate consists of six parts:
receiving the command, not accepting, receiving again, the Buddha’s exhortation, immediate acceptance, and the conclusion; all are as stated in the text.
From the section on "Holding the Ground" (*Dharaṇī*) onwards, it concerns the merits of hearing this chapter, and so forth.
Regarding "the peerless" (asama-sama): the minds of the nine realms of existence cannot equal this principle, whereas the mind of the Buddha-dharma realm can equal it; thus, it is peerless yet equal.

Furthermore, the principle of ultimate reality (*atyanta-niṣṭhā*) is peerless; because one initially generates the resolve for enlightenment by taking this ultimate principle as the object of focus, one is able to equalize with that principle, and is therefore said to be "equal to the peerless" (*asama-sama*).
Furthermore, since both the mind and principle are ungraspable, what thing could be equal to what other thing such that one speaks of "the unequally equal"?
Both the mind and principle are ineffable; yet, speaking of the ineffable, one says that this mind is equal to this principle, and thus it is called "the unequally equal."
The first [explanation] is a horizontal interpretation; the second is a vertical interpretation; and the third is an interpretation that is neither horizontal nor vertical, and so forth.
Regarding the "Explanation of the Dhāraṇī Chapter": *dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*zongchi*). Total retention means that evil does not arise and good is not lost.
Furthermore, it can be translated as "able to obstruct" and "able to maintain. These two mean that it can maintain the wholesome and obstruct the unwholesome.
The third meaning is that it can obstruct extreme unwholesomeness and maintain the wholesome of the middle way.
The fourfold assembly’s various sūtras differ in their prescriptions and prohibitions: some are exclusively for treating illness, such as the *Nāda-gṛhapati-sūtra*;
some are exclusively for protecting the Dharma, such as this present text;
and some are exclusively for extinguishing transgressions, such as the Vaipulya sūtras.

Some mantras are used universally for curing illness, extinguishing transgressions, and protecting scriptures, such as the *Avalokiteśvara-āhvāna* (The Invocation of Avalokiteśvara). Others, such as the Great Mantra, the Unsurpassed Mantra, and the Peerless Mantra, are not for curing illness, extinguishing transgressions, or protecting scriptures; yet if one is comprehensive in approach, these should also be practiced concurrently. However, if discussing them specifically, one must fortunately rely upon the scriptures and not deviate from the teachings, and so forth.

Some masters say that "mantra" (zhòu) is the name of a king of ghosts; by invoking the name of this king, his tribes respect their lord and dare not commit transgressions, and thus one is able to subdue all malevolent spirits—this is the first [explanation].

Some say that a mantra is like a secret code within an army; when the code is correctly recited, no one questions it, but if it is incorrect, one is immediately seized and punished. If one does not comply with the mantra, one's head shall split into seven pieces; if one complies with the mantra, there shall be no fault. (2)

Some say that as for "incantation" (*dhāraṇī*), it refers to the secret and silent subduing of evil so that the evil naturally ceases. It is like a lowly person who flees from this country to another country and falsely claims to be a prince; the other country gives him a princess as his wife, yet he is prone to anger and difficult to manage.

A wise man came from that country, and the master went to speak with him. The man said to the master: "If you must speak verses when in a fit of anger, let them say: 'Having no kin, you wander in a foreign land, deceiving all people; since coarse food is your constant lot, why trouble yourself further by giving way to anger?'"
When these verses were spoken, his anger subsided in silence, and he did not become angry again thereafter; the master and all the people heard only these verses, yet none understood their meaning.
The mantra is also like this: it secretly and silently wards off evil, while others remain unaware of it—this is the third point.

Some say that a mantra is the secret language of all Buddhas; it is like a king who calls for "saindhava," which none of his subordinates can identify, yet only a wise minister understands what it means.

Mantras are also like this: they are merely a single dharma that universally possesses all powers. These four—curing illness, eliminating transgressions, generating goodness, and attaining accord with the Path—exist for this reason;
thus, the original sounds are preserved, and the translators did not translate them because their intention lay therein.
In an evil age, propagating this sutra brings many afflictions and obstacles; therefore, one protects it with mantras so that the Way may circulate.

The text consists of four parts: first, questioning regarding the merit of upholding the sutra; second, answering that it is exceedingly great; third, requesting protection by means of mantras; and fourth, the benefits gained upon hearing this chapter.
The first question is as in the text.
The second answer involves a comparative evaluation:
"Is the original question many?"
The answer is that they are very numerous; the merits enumerated therein are as stated in the text.
Regarding the request to recite the mantras, there are five sections:
first, Bhaiṣajyarāja; second, Śūradatta; third, Vaiśravaṇa; fourth, Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and fifth, the ten daughters.
The Medicine King [Chapter] consists of four parts:
first, the request; second, the exposition; third, the praise; and fourth, the seal.
The subsequent examples consist of three parts each, as shown in the text.
The ten daughters constitute five sections:
first, the enumeration of names; second, the request for exposition; third, the praise; fourth, the vow; and fifth, the seal.
"Yakṣa" is translated as "swift demon," and "Rākṣasa" is translated as "man-eating demon"; these two classes are those governed by the Northern Quarter.
"Pūtana" refers to a fever-demon; "Kiṃkara" refers to a corpse-raising demon; both humans and yakṣas may possess these demons. "Vetāla" refers to a red-colored demon;

"Khaṇḍarohā" refers to a yellow-colored demon (the specific nature of which is not yet detailed); "Umbarī" refers to a black-colored demon (the specific nature of which is not yet detailed); and "Apasmāra" refers to a blue-colored demon.

When a branch of the *ari* tree falls to the ground, it naturally breaks into seven pieces as a matter of natural law (*dharmatā*). Killing one's father, killing one's mother, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha constitute these three immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*).

Regarding foreign oils, they crush sesame seeds until worms are produced and then press them together; this is done with the intent to extract more juice for greater richness, yet it is a particularly grave fault.

To weigh out light and take in heavy with scales and measures is the height of deceitful theft; in recent times, there have been those who used small measures to dispense goods and large measures to receive them, having the character of "Zhen" (Vibration) engraved on their backs—this offense, too, is no light matter.

**Exposition on the Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment.** The causal conditions for this chapter are derived from another sutra: In the past, during the final dharma age (*paścima-dharma*), there were four bhikṣus who conceived an extremely profound and earnest reverence for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Although they unrolled and studied its secret teachings, the nectar had not yet moistened them. Day and night they remained upright in sincerity, never forgetting it for even a moment.
They sighed, saying: "If it is not for the right person, [what is the use?]"
Is this place not unsuitable?
The world is turbulent and sorrowful; stillness and dispersion are at odds. If even seeking leisure requires one to weary of and abandon it, how much more so for one who reveres the Way?

Thereupon, they formed a covenant to dwell among the mountains and forests, their aspirations delighting in the wisdom of the Buddha. As they lived in seclusion for many days, their clothing and provisions were gradually exhausted; they were often troubled by the need for sustenance, lacking nothing at no time. To have but a single meal with a rattling sound in the throat would cause one to abandon a journey of ten thousand *li*; to eat but once in nine out of ten days would compel one to humble their soaring ambitions—how can this not be spoken of?
One of them said: "We four paupers have not even the means to preserve our own bodies; where, then, should the Dharma be entrusted?
You three gentlemen need only devote your lives to the Way and need not worry about the court; as for me alone, I shall surrender this body and strength, vowing to provide whatever is required."

Thereupon, shaking his mendicant’s staff, he sought alms from door to door to sustain himself; from spring until winter, he traveled in a continuous cycle, beginning again and again, like a servant attending to his master, remaining indifferent to both hardship and comfort, without joy or resentment.
Three individuals were able to manifest their sincerity; their merit was perfected and their task accomplished, such that the benefit they bring to this world shall endure for immeasurable lifetimes.
As for the one person who has frequently traversed the human realm and repeatedly encountered sensory objects, his vessel is as yet unbaked by fire and difficult to preserve.

Once, he happened upon a king going out in a carriage; the horses were packed closely together and the banners and flags were magnificent and dazzling. He gave rise to thoughts and conceived a longing for that glory. Because his merit had been cultivated through such mental cultivation, he received its retribution in accordance with his thoughts, constantly becoming a king among humans and in the heavens. Although his blessings were immeasurable, they were nonetheless finite.
The three men met at the assembly where they had attained the Way and deliberated, saying:

"Our success in escaping the cage and the enclosure was due to this King; yet he remains addicted to karmic retribution and increases conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*). Once he dies from this, he will no longer be king, and it will be truly difficult to rescue him as he sinks into the pit of fire. Fortunately, before he suffers such pain, he is precisely the right time for his conversion."

One of them said: "This king is addicted to desire and furthermore holds wrong views; unless we use the hook of affection, there is no way to pull him out. Let one become a beautiful wife and the other a clever son; since the words of a wife and a son must be obeyed, if we apply this method of conversion appropriately, he will surely reform his heterodoxy."
The wife was the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara;
the two sons of former times are now the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata; and the king of former times is now the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa.

Therefore, with the white tuft of hair summoning from the east, he ascended the Purple Terrace and led [the assembly] westward; through divine mantras he protected the sutra so that it might circulate and bring great benefit. Because he recounted the prior karmic conditions of the Four Holy Ones, this is titled "The Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment."
Furthermore, "Sublime Adornment" refers to the adornment of the sense faculties by the merits of the Sublime Dharma.

This king had a karmic affinity for the Sublime Dharma in past lives; as the seeds of the Path were perfumed and matured, his faculties ought to have been purified. Although he has not yet attained [full realization] in this life, the principle must inevitably reach its fulfillment. Thus, through the resonance of spiritual auspiciousness, his illustrious name was established early on.

For example, although Subhūti had not yet attained the state of being "without contention," he was already called "Born of Emptiness" (Śūnyatā-ja). Thus, the subsequent text states that he "attained the Samādhi Adorned with Pure Merit"; for this reason, he is named "King Wondrous Adornment."

The preceding chapter explained the protection through mantras; this chapter explains the protection of persons. If even the protection of persons is thus effective, the protection through mantras is all the more efficacious;

this serves as a universal exhortation for the circulation [of the teaching]. The text consists of six parts: first, clarifying the origin of the matter; second, dual presentation of the agent and the object; third, the skillful means of the transformer; fourth, the benefits gained by those being transformed; fifth, concluding by correlating the ancient and the present; sixth, awakening to the Way upon hearing this chapter.
The fundamental matter is as stated in the text.
From the passage "In that Buddha-dharma" onwards, the second section provides a dual heading for the agent and the object.
It names both the single person to be transformed and the three persons who transform, specifically revealing the merit, wisdom, six perfections, and four great vows of the two sons.
Other sutras designate these as the ten pāramitās, which constitute the horizontal dharma-gate;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitute the vertical dharma-gate.
In other sutras, these are considered the primary path, while the practices of cultivation are considered the auxiliary path.
In this present sutra, the ten perfections (daśapāramitā) are designated as the primary path, while these [other samādhis] are called "auxiliaries to the path" (bodhipakṣa).

Since the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) already contains samādhi, and each section within the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) also contains samādhi, the separate listing of the seven samādhis serves merely to extensively manifest various dharma-gates.
From "At that time, that Buddha" onwards is the third section, the skillful means of transformation, which consists of three parts:
first, the arrival of the time;
second, the discussion; [and third, the actual transformation].
Third, the manifestation [of the Buddha].

Regarding those who arrive at the initial stage: when that Buddha appears in the world, he constantly proclaims the True Dharma; if the conditions for the king are weak, it is not yet the right time, but if one were to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, then it would indeed be the right time.
The text states: "That Buddha was about to guide [beings] by preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*"; this is precisely its meaning. Second, regarding the discussion:
