when Wenzzi informed his mother that the time had come, the mother urged him to convert his father; the son lamented that he had left the house of heterodox views; and the mother reproached him for his lack of concern—everything is as stated in the text.
From "Then these two sons" onwards is the third section, the manifestation of transformations.
This manifestation of transformations should consist of the eighteen miraculous powers, which may be explained in full.
From "At that time, the father saw his sons" onwards is the fourth section, the benefits obtained by those being transformed.

The text consists of ten sections: First, the son’s subduing of the teacher. When the king beheld the heterodox transformations—whether one or two in number—they were narrow and crude; yet upon seeing what his son had accomplished, he marveled at such an unprecedented feat. Trusting his son, he submitted to the teacher and asked, "Who is this teacher? I too wish to see him."

Second, the father king had already gained faith, and the eighty-four thousand women in the palace were likewise matured; they informed their mother and offered congratulations, wishing for him to be released so he might leave the home life, and the mother also granted her permission.
Third, he repeatedly exhorted his parents that now was precisely the right time, for a Buddha is difficult to encounter.
Fourth, as the merit of his transformative work had already become manifest, the Buddha praised his meritorious virtues.
Regarding the "Lotus Samādhi," it encompasses all dharmas and returns them to the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇa*), as previously explained.

Regarding "departing from the evil destinies" (*apāya*): while it is conventionally understood that the three miserable realms constitute the evil destinies, a comprehensive discussion reveals that all twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) involve a deviation from truth and the arising of delusion; thus, they are all evil destinies. To depart from them all now is precisely to attain the twenty-five samādhis and to shatter the twenty-five states of existence.
Regarding "the Samādhi of the Buddha’s Assembly": it is the secret treasury wherein the Buddhas assemble; it is the sphere of activity of the Buddhas alone, not of others.
Fifth, they all went to the Buddha's abode, heard the Dharma as an offering, and rejoiced upon seeing the auspicious signs.
Sixth, the Buddha bestows the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Seventh, leaving the household life to practice the path.
Eighth, praising the two sons.
9. The Buddha recounts the excellence of his practice.
10. He praises his own vow.

The Buddha extols that spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) possess great significance; spiritual friends are able to perform the work of a Buddha—these are the external protectors who serve as spiritual friends.
"Showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening" refers to the spiritual friend who provides instruction;
"namely, transforming and guiding them so that they may attain the vision of the Buddha" refers to the spiritual friend who practices together;
and "causing them to enter into bodhi" refers to the spiritual friend of the ultimate reality and the true mark.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "A virtuous friend is like a chaste and good wife"—this refers to the meaning of external protection (*bāhya-rakṣā*).
Furthermore, "a virtuous friend is like kinsmen and wealth"—this refers to the meaning of practicing together (*sahāya*).
Moreover, "a virtuous friend is like a merchant leader"—this refers to the meaning of instruction (*avavāda*).
Furthermore, the spiritual friend is like a child lying in his father’s lap; this is the meaning of the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality).
From the passage "The Buddha addressed the great assembly" onwards, there is a synthesis of the ancient and the present: first, the synthesis; second, the concluding praise of the two bodhisattvas.
"Regarding 'This was said' and below," the hearing of this chapter and the attainment of the Way are as written in the text.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva": the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* both use the name "Pianji" (遍吉), while this sutra uses "Puxian" (普賢); all are Chinese translations of the Sanskrit *Samantabhadra*, which means "Universal Goodness" (*Puxian*).

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "I vow that within this defiled and evil world, I shall practice the bodhisattva path to bring it to adornment and purity; my practice must surely surpass that of all other bodhisattvas."
The Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"By these causes and conditions, I now change your name and call you Samantabhadra.
This is the meaning of the three *siddhāntas*; it is further an explanation by way of causes and conditions, and it is also how he attained his name through his practice and vows.
From the foundations of mindfulness up to the four roots of goodness, they are collectively termed "Universal Good" (Samantabhadra).

Specifically, regarding the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which is adjacent to the Truth and proximate to the Sages, it is designated as "Good" (*bhadra*); this is what is taught within the Tripiṭaka.

Now, to clarify the summit of the path of subduing (*vibhava-mārga*): its cause being all-pervasive is termed "Universal" (*pu*), and its position following the path of severance (*prahāṇa-mārga*) and bordering upon the ultimate sage is termed "Worthy" (*xian*).

If the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) represent the beginning of the path of subduing, they are neither the summit nor all-pervasive; they border on the very first stage of the sages, being neither subsequent nor ultimate. Even the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) is not yet all-pervasive or ultimate, let alone the preceding stages.

Now, regarding the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi), it occupies the summit among all stages of subduing; because the path of subduing is all-pervasive, it is called "Universal" (P'u). Because the path of abandonment has almost reached its end, with only a small measure remaining, and because it borders upon the ultimate limit, it is called "Worthy" (Hsien). As the *Śāstra* cites the moon on the fourteenth night being like the moon on the fifteenth night, this meaning is clear.
This is an explanation of the final stage, that of Samantabhadra, according to the位次 (stages) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

"Exhortation" (*quanfa*) is a term expressing devotion to the Dharma. Having heard the beginning and end of this sutra in its entirety from afar while residing in that land, [Samantabhadra] desires to ensure that his own practice and his transformation of others continue forever without end; thus, he comes from the east and from the west to offer exhortation, embodying the four *siddhāntas*, and so forth.
The text says: "First, for the sake of making offerings to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I manifest my own body; if they see my body, they will experience great joy.
Second, because they have seen me, they will further increase their diligent practice and immediately attain samādhi and dhāraṇī.
Third, because they have attained this dhāraṇī, no non-human being can destroy them, nor will they be deluded or disturbed by women."
"Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems, fully endowed with the path of Samantabhadra—this is the fourth.
Such explicit passages as these constitute the four *siddhāntas*, through which [the Buddha] comes to exhort and inspire [beings].
The Master judges that the section on circulation is divided into three parts:
from the nineteenth verse onwards, spanning three and a half chapters, he exhorts circulation by highlighting the great power of the sutra;
in the five chapters beginning with the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Medicine King," he exhorts circulation by highlighting the great power of the bodhisattvas' transformative path.
This chapter highlights the greatness of Samantabhadra’s power of vow to encourage the circulation [of this teaching].
It is divided into four sections:
first, the arrival;...
2. Exhortation; 3. Narration of the arousal [of the thought of enlightenment];
4. Benefits of the arousal.
First, the Sūtra master’s introduction of the arrival is threefold:
first, the superior offering;
second, the downward transformation.
Third, the Cultivation of Reverence.

"Sovereignty" refers to the unity of principle; "supernatural powers" refer to the unity of practice; "majestic virtue" refers to the unity of the person; and "renown" refers to the unity of the teaching.

Furthermore, "sovereignty" (vaśitā) is permanence; "supernatural powers" (abhijñā) are bliss; "majestic virtue" (tejas) is selfhood; and "renown" (yaśas) is purity. When expressed in this way, there is one [essence] and four [attributes]; no virtue is lacking, which constitutes the meaning of sovereignty.
By the power of purity, flowers rain down; by the power of joy, music is performed; by the power of supernormal faculties, the earth trembles.
By the power of mastery, they cause rain to fall according to their will—raining wherever they go and performing music wherever they move.
Just as a great dragon flies without ceasing, with clouds and rain streaming forth from its body and sides in endless succession,
so too Samantabhadra and his retinue come by means of the bodies of bodhisattvas, employing the power of the four virtues.
The fourfold exhortation to practice:
First, regarding the manner in which he personally made offerings at the places he traversed, the matter is as follows.

From the passage beginning with "Furthermore, together with the devas and nāgas" onwards, it concerns his downward transformation and benefitting of others at the places he traversed; he manifested the forms of the eight classes of beings according to what was appropriate for each, briefly employing two powers according to their respective capacities—the matter is as follows.
Third is the cultivation of reverence, which involves turning the body and prostrating with the face toward [the object], as described in the text.
Exhortation to practice consists of two parts:
first, exhortation through inquiry; and second, exhortation through instruction.
2. Encouragement through Vows.
There is a question and an answer.

As for the questioner: having heard from afar that the sutra was concluded, his longing for the Dharma remained unceasing; with the resolve to travel far in mind and the intent to provide encouragement, he requests [the teaching] once more.

The former discourse exhorted the practice of self-cultivation, while this further request exhorts the propagation for the sake of transforming others. If the Tathāgata grants permission, these two paths shall be expounded once more, radiating infinite light; therefore, he makes this dual request.
The Buddha’s response consists of three parts: first, a general summary; second, a detailed exposition; and third, a conclusion.
The names of the four dharmas are listed individually as they appear in the text.
Since the request was made in pairs, the Tathāgata skillfully responded by briefly citing four [categories] to encompass all others.
What are they? The essentials of these four dharmas encompass both the orthodox and the comprehensive. What are they?

Although the Buddha is without partiality, if one can distance oneself from evil and follow the good, turn back from delusion to return to the correct path, open up provisional knowledge and vision, and manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, then one will accord with the Sage’s heart and be protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
When the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, Prajñā illuminates; this is the planting of the roots of all virtues.
It is also the entry into the stage of the right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), where there is no distraction, no attachment to flavors, and neither grasping nor rejecting.
This is also the arousal of the resolve to rescue sentient beings.
One should know that these four [aspects] and the "opening of the provisional to reveal the real" are identical in substance despite differing in name; they are non-dual and without distinction.
Furthermore, "being protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" refers to the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"Planting the roots of all virtues" indicates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
"vowing to rescue sentient beings" awakens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
and "entering the stage of right determination" is entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The essentials of the Trace Gate (jìmén) are encompassed by these four.

Furthermore, the Trace has its Source (běn); because [the Buddha] proceeds from the Source through opening, showing, awakening, and entering, there is consequently the opening, showing, awakening, and entering within the Trace.

Now, by revealing the traces (*jia*), the fundamental reality (*ben*) is manifested; thus, the fundamental and the trace are neither two nor distinct. To answer his request for the correct teaching, the four dharmas clarify the meaning.
To answer his request for the propagation [of the Dharma], the methods of propagation consist of only three or four: "Resolving to save sentient beings" is entering the Tathāgata’s chamber;
"Entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and being protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" is donning the Tathāgata’s robe.
"To plant the roots of all virtues" is to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat;
this is the essential method for widespread proclamation, which is threefold within the four [practices].
"To resolve to rescue sentient beings" is the vow of the Practice of Peaceful Living.
"Entering the stage of right determination" is the practice of mental ease;
"planting the roots of all virtues" is the practice of verbal ease;
and "receiving protection and mindfulness" is the practice of physical ease. One should know that the latter four [practices] are identical to the former four.

First, I shall respond to his two requests: by citing four [scriptures] to encompass one sutra, I shall re-expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and proclaim this scripture once more. Such is the significance of my encouragement for him who has come from afar.
Third, the conclusion: after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one will certainly obtain this sutra.
As it was said in the old [translation]: "If one can practice four dharmas in future ages, one will always have this sutra in hand."

Now, this is not so; for the preceding text states, "The meaning of the true reality of all dharmas has already been explained for you," and it further says, "Causing all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

In essence, the true substance of the *Lotus Sūtra* is that one who can practice these four dharmas will necessarily attain this understanding; thus, "understanding" (*jie*) is termed the "sūtra. This concludes the inquiry regarding the request for the correct teaching. Furthermore, if one can employ this understanding and transmit it to others, those others will attain this faith and understanding and become the first type of person who relies [on the teaching]. They will then be able to attain true understanding and become the second, third, and fourth types of persons who rely [on the teaching]. This concludes the inquiry regarding the request for the circulation [of the teaching]. If this meaning is not perceived, is it not a waste to produce other interpretations?
From "He addressed the Buddha" onwards is the second section, the Exhortation through Vows.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the protection of persons; second, the protection of the Dharma.
There are six ways of protecting people:
first, warding off external calamities. Initially, this refers to warding off calamities in general; thus, the phrase "so that no one seeking an opportunity can find an opening" refers to this.
Next, regarding the specific removal of those calamities, it is stated that there are twelve instances of what is not correct.

Second, as for teaching them the internal Dharma, there are generally three stages of instruction: first, practicing standing recitation, whereby one mounts a six-tusked white elephant to comfort their mind;
next, practicing seated contemplation, whereby one again mounts the six-tusked elephant to instruct them in the sutras and grant them samādhi.

“Dhāraṇī” refers to revolving from the provisional into emptiness; “hundreds of thousands of revolutions” refers to revolving from emptiness back out into the provisional; and “expedient means” (upāya) refers to these two serving as the path of expedient means to attain entry into the Middle Way, the primary truth of ultimate meaning.
Thereafter, for three weeks, he practiced with single-minded diligence; furthermore, riding upon his six tusks, he provided instruction, benefit, and joy by reciting the mantra as written.
Third, he covered [the assembly] with his supernormal powers; whether hearing or upholding [the teaching], it was none other than the power of his spiritual transformations, as written.

4. Showing the superior cause: if one can act as a Dharma teacher in these five ways, one is the seed planted by the Buddhas of the three periods of time for the purpose of ripening and liberation; such a person will attain liberation together with all future Buddhas, and is therefore said to "share in the conduct of Samantabhadra."
This person has already planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas; therefore, it is said that they have "deeply planted roots of goodness.
This person has been matured by the present Buddha; therefore, it is said that the Buddha "places his hand upon their head."

Fifth, the demonstration of the proximate fruit: merely being able to copy [the text] results in proximity to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; possessing the five qualities of a Dharma-master leads to the Tuṣita Heaven, as stated in the text.
Sixth, the summary: this is the section beginning with "Therefore, the wise person... and so forth.
From "World-Honored One, by my present supernatural power" onwards is the second section, the vow to protect the Dharma, as written in the text.

The third is the description of the one who initiates [the teaching]; that is, the Tathāgata elevates the superior to describe and establish the inferior, thereby increasing the vigor and courage of the practitioner to propagate it widely.

First, regarding the protection of the Dharma, he said: "Since you are thus able to provide great benefit externally and accumulate compassion internally, and have practiced such protection for many kalpas, I too shall protect this Dharma through the supernatural power of the Buddha—how much more so should you?"
As stated in the text.
From the passage beginning with "If there be a person" onwards, it describes those whom he protects; although not in sequential order, the intent is fully established.

Regarding the statement, "One should know that such a person sees Śākyamuni Buddha," this describes his manifestation of the body and the teaching of the Dharma: if they can still see my fruition-body endowed with myriad virtues, how much more so you, who in the stage of causes are a six-tusked white elephant?
If even he has heard the sūtras in their entirety directly from the Buddha’s own mouth, how much more so you, who have forgotten the words and phrases taught by others?
If even he was praised by the Buddha’s own mouth, stroked by his hand, and covered by the Buddha’s robe, how much more so you, who are protected by the dhāraṇīs of others?
From the passage "not being greedily attached to worldly pleasures" onwards, the reasons for [the practice] are set forth.

Within the extensive presentation of these reasons, it describes the superior causes: being free from all faults and evils, having few desires and knowing contentment, and cultivating the practices of Samantabhadra.
From the passage beginning "If, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa," the text describes the attainment of the proximate fruit.
If such a person will certainly attain the distant fruit upon reaching the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), how much more so the proximate fruit?
Furthermore, one obtains its proximate fruits even in the present life, not merely rebirth in heaven.
From the passage "If a person slights and reviles... onwards, it describes how this [practice] can ward off external calamities.

The Buddha extensively reveals the offenses of those who would disparage [this teaching], so that they may recognize their transgressions and surely reform them, rather than causing mutual disturbance. It is not only that those who uphold the sutra find it difficult to extinguish [their faults]; even for those who wish to disparage it, merit arises. When there is neither disparagement nor difficulty, both parties abide in peace and happiness. This vast salvation is impartial; it is the ultimate expression of compassion.
From the passage "One should rise to meet him from afar as if revering a Buddha," the merit of those who establish faith is described.
Fourth, from the section beginning with "Having spoken these words," is the text concerning the arising of benefits.
First, the benefit of hearing the chapter: "The Dharani of Revolving" refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*), while "Possessing the Path of Samantabhadra" refers to the tenth stage;
second, the benefit of hearing the sutra: this is the "Great Assembly’s Joy."
"Rejoicing" is as previously explained.
Why, then, is he still referred to here as a śrāvaka?
This is merely because the compiler of the sutra has preserved his original status.
Furthermore, the author of the sūtra refers to him as a "Mahāyāna śrāvaka," thereby making even more manifest the meaning that he causes all beings to hear the sound of the Buddha-way.
*Wenju* on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Fascicle Ten, Part Two.
